comment.value:
Thank you for your positive feedback! We appreciate that you found our use of SAEs interesting and novel. 

**Lack of ablations on SAEs(size,corpora etc), and similarly for reader LLM, and also diversity of datasets..how much does the SAE or reader LLM impact quality of embeddings, have you done any ablations on them?**

Please see the "Exploring different SAEs" section in the meta-commentary.

In terms of testing on diverse datasets, we focused primarily on model-related datasets (prompts, responses, training data) as we believe understanding model-related data is underexplored, but we emphasise that the SAE embedding is general purpose and included a few non-model-related datasets (e.g. CivilComments, synthetic datasets).

**A lot of the results are in the appendix, so there's a lot of back and forth while reading.**

Please see the "Clarity" section in the meta-commentary.

**The paper primarily uses chatstyle prompts, have you guys explored any other datasets or prompts that could be treated as somewhat out-of-distribution in dataset-diffing and correlation experiments?**

Yes. For dataset-diffing, we use a movie genres dataset for our ground-truth evaluation. We diff all the movie descriptions within a genre with 500 randomly selected movie descriptions outside the genre, finding that the top latent difference often aligns with the ground truth (e.g. “Action” genre - “Action movie plot developments and dramatic confrontations”). See Table 1 for more examples.

On correlations, we search for highly correlated latent pairs in the CivilComments dataset, finding that we can surface instances of bias (e.g. sexism, racism). This makes sense given that CivilComments is often used in toxicity classification benchmarks, but for the uninformed dataset user, these insights would point to unknown problems within the dataset. We provide examples in Figure 4 (top). 

**It is known that malicious texts in the pretraining do poison LLMs, how can we adapt this framework to large scale corpora filtering?**

This is an interesting point. While we did not explicitly have this use case in mind, our Tulu-3 case study demonstrates a viable path for detecting spurious triggers in documents (prompt-response pairs in this case, but it could similarly work for normal documents if we split the document). Empirically, we’ve observed that rarer/undertrained tokens that may be used as triggers seem to activate “random” SAE latents, so it is very plausible that this will be found when we look for unrelated latents that co-occur. Given that we can detect injected correlations at very small percentages (0.1%-1.0%, see Section 4.2 & Appendix G.2), we would be excited to see if we can detect the poisoned pretraining documents as recently described in Souly et. al [1]. 

**Could we improve current dense embeddings by training SAEs on them, or by taking a trained SAE from a model like Llama3-70B or Gemma (which already have SAEs) and converting it to dense embeddings with something like LLM2Vec?**

In Section 2, we cited prior works that have trained SAEs on dense embeddings, finding that they do enable controllable retrieval and generate better hypotheses for classifiers. The key difference between their SAE trained on a dense text embedding (that represents a whole text) versus ours, which is trained on a decoder-only LLM’s token-level activations, would be that the former focuses on the general meaning of the text, while the latter (with our max-pooling aggregation) focuses on “is concept X present”. These are fundamentally different representations of text, so it would depend on the use case.

In fact, we have some preliminary results in Appendix D where we investigate information present in our SAE embedding that is not present in dense embeddings. For each SAE latent, we explore how predictable its activations are from dense embeddings. We find that some SAE latents are not predictable from dense embeddings, and qualitatively, it seems that our SAEs capture the presence of granular properties better.

**Feature relabelling is critical, what if we dont know the distribution of the data so we cant recorrect them which is plausible in the deployment, how much will the quality of embeddings degrade?**

While feature relabeling certainly helps to make labels more specific for the given dataset, we note that even just using pre-existing labels, SAEs fare reasonably well. For instance, in our retrieval task, we benchmark SAEs alongside existing dense embedding baselines on a variety of datasets, both in and out of distribution (the SAE was trained on LMSYS-1M chat conversations). Just using the SAE’s existing feature labels, we find that it is on par with most baselines even on more out-of-distribution datasets like Reddit short stories.

[1] “Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples” - https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07192

**Clustering...results are only reported for one algorithm. Demonstrating consistent results across multiple algorithms would increase the reliability of the claim.**

We chose to use spectral clustering on the Jaccard similarity matrix, as we think that is the most principled clustering algorithm for clustering the presence of features. We binarize because the absolute scale of activations may differ across latents, so any algorithm relying on Euclidean distance (e.g. k-means) would not make much sense without normalization. We focused on one clustering algorithm to emphasize that SAEs can give novel insights via their controllability. It is possible that different clustering algorithms (e.g. density-based) would have different insights, and we are excited to explore these questions in future work.

**...the SAE retrieval setup introduces higher computational overhead due to latent-query dense similarity matching. Exploring alternative strategies that are more efficient would make the method more practical for real-world deployment.**

One alternative could be BM25-style search over latent labels, which would be more sensitive to the exact label and might require us to explore a different labelling strategy, e.g. optimize labels for the presence of key tokens. This could indeed be more efficient, and “keyword”-based SAE labels could even work better; we plan to explore this route in future work and appreciate the direction.

For now, we have more explicitly stated in the limitations that we do not claim the SAE method to be more computationally efficient than just dense similarity matching over the dataset directly. We’ve also added retrieval results in Figure 6 for the SAE method without LLM reranking of the matched latents, which removes any LLM from the retrieval pipeline and thus reduces computational cost, at a slight cost in performance.

**Results are reported for only one SAE model. Testing multiple SAE models would make the findings more reliable and better support the claim that SAEs are a good choice.**

Please see the "Exploring different SAEs" section in the meta-commentary.

**...Testing different prompt formulations for the LLM stages and baselines would clarify how sensitive the results are to prompt design.**

Since our most LLM-intensive baseline was the diffing baseline (marked as LLM-S in the updated manuscript), we provide another baseline that adopts a different prompting strategy (denoted LLM-C). While both baselines generate differences from the model responses per prompt, LLM-C uses a different summarization approach, clustering the differences and generating hypotheses from cluster labels.

As shown in Figure 2, LLM-C generally outperforms LLM-S in average frequency difference but still underperforms SAE hypotheses. Additionally, in Figure 13, we show that SAE hypotheses continue to have more coverage than LLM-C hypotheses on multi-model comparisons, which is consistent with LLM-S hypotheses. We further note that our prompt for the difference discovery step was carried over from Vibecheck [2], a prior work that aims to identify qualitative differences between two LLMs, with some light edits to account for multiple models. 

**The analysis workflows depend heavily on another LLM...suggesting that SAEs alone are not sufficient for the intended tasks. Designing experiments that evaluate the effectiveness of SAEs in isolation would provide a clearer understanding of their independent capabilities and limitations.**

We acknowledge that the diffing workflow makes use of LLMs to relabel and summarize latents. However, we also highlight that our ground-truth experiments were constructed to evaluate SAE latents on their own. Even just relying on the latent descriptions provided by Goodfire (which were not made with tones or movie descriptions in mind), we already observe useful latent differences that point to the ground truth difference, as shown in Table 1.

Our current correlations workflow does not require LLMs (they were only used for verification experiments). Our clustering and retrieval workflows can optionally use LLMs to improve query-label matching, but are entirely possible with just semantic search over the labels (e.g. our GSM8k results used semantic search). We’ve also added retrieval results in Figure 6 for the SAE method without LLM reranking of the matched latents—denoted as “SAE 70B (no rerank)”--which removes any LLM from the retrieval pipeline and thus reduces computational cost, at a slight cost in performance.

We included LLM steps to standardize analysis workflows and minimize manual checking, but the latter is an open alternative.

In light of the OpenReview circumstances, it is unfortunate that we were unable to get feedback from the reviewers on our updated manuscript. However, we sincerely hope our changes have addressed reviewers’ concerns and provide a final summary of the discussion here:

We want to thank the reviewers for appreciating the practical utility of our work, the rigor of our experiments, and the creativity of our approach. The main concern common across all reviewers was the lack of clarity due to frequent references to the appendix. As described in our meta-comment below, we have used the additional page to move key results to the main text, as well as added explanations for points of common confusion for reviewers (e.g., latent relabelling). Another common reviewer concern was the false positive rates of our hypothesis generation tasks, diffing (Section 4.1) and correlations (Section 4.2). We have added experiments quantifying the false positive rates for both diffing and correlations, finding that SAEs are similarly or (often) less noisy than baselines on tested datasets. We have also added baselines for diffing and correlations that further support the strength of SAEs over existing methods. 

We summarize individual reviews below:

**Reviewer v8eo (score: 6)**

This reviewer’s feedback centered around the clarity of the paper. Our current manuscript has been substantially revised to sufficiently address their concerns, such as reduced cross-referencing to the appendix and the addition of key details (latent relabeling procedure).

They were also concerned about how noisy hypotheses generated from the SAE are. We have addressed this by adding the experiments on false-positive rates for diffing and correlations, as well as clarifying in the response how our case study results were obtained.

**Reviewer N1em (score: 2)**

This reviewer’s feedback centered around providing more rigor to experiments.

We have since addressed these concerns through the following additional experiments:
- Diffing
    - Added quantitative results for the ground-truth experiments (movies and tones dataset, Section 4.1), showing SAEs can recover ground-truth differences between datasets.
    - Added new LLM baseline (Figure 2) for comparing model outputs
    - Quantified false positive rate (Figure 12) and overall coverage (Figure 13) of differences for model responses, showing SAEs outperform baselines on multi-model comparisons and similarly on two-model comparisons
- Correlations
    - Added an experiment to show that the LLM baseline is unreliable, as whether it can recover the ground truth depends on the dataset order
    - Added quantitative results for the judge-verified correlation of SAE-discovered and baseline-discovered pairs (Figure 4), showing that SAEs have a lower false discovery rate as they identify latent pairs that are more highly correlated. 
- Retrieval
    - Added results for a Llama 8B SAE (Figure 6)
- Different SAEs: showed preliminary experiments comparing the F1 score from using Llama 8B and Llama 70B SAE activations to classify properties (based on latent description) in various datasets, as a general way to benchmark an SAE’s quality for data analysis (Appendix J)

We again thank the reviewer for providing additional experiments, which we have incorporated to further strengthen the rigor of our claim that SAEs are effective in data analysis tasks. Our paper presents a promising direction for unstructured data analysis of model-related data, which we hope will encourage future studies on using model data to discover unknown or surprising behaviors.

**Reviewer bVzV (score: 8)**

This reviewer highlighted that the work was “interesting and novel”. Their feedback centered on the choice of SAEs. We have added retrieval results for a different Llama 8B SAE, as well as provided some preliminary experiments on SAE latent F1 score for 8B and 70B SAEs. We have also addressed their clarity concerns.

**Reviewer 3QR3 (score: 4)**

The 2 weaknesses pointed out both center around the clarity of the paper.
> Organization and readability can be improved; heavy cross-referencing to tables/figures disrupts flow.

We have majorly edited the paper for readability, reducing cross-referencing to the Appendix.

> The procedure for producing interpretable activation vectors is not very clear.

We have addressed this confusion by expanding Section 3 (methods) to detail the latent relabelling procedure, which seemed to be the main confusion for the reviewer.

We believe we have sufficiently addressed their clarity concerns, and given that there were no stated concerns about experiments, we hope the reviewer would have an improved assessment of the paper.


Overall, we once again thank the reviewers for their detailed and constructive feedback, which have inspired what we feel is a great improvement to the paper. Thank you!

Thank you to all reviewers for your thoughtful reviews! We are happy that all the reviewers viewed our work as “interesting” (bVzV, 3QR3), “creative” (N1em), or “novel” (v8eo, bVzV) and are excited about potential directions and improvements. We have since taken the feedback and added more results focused on improving the clarity and rigor (quantitative verification, false positive rate) of our claims. We’ve addressed specific concerns in individual responses, and here we summarize the common themes and changes made:

**Clarity** (v8eo, N1em, bVzV, 3QR3)

Many reviewers pointed out that the paper was difficult to follow due to cross-referencing with the Appendix. We have since taken this feedback and made major revisions for clarity.
We brought these key results into the main text, using the extra page:

1. Ground truth verification for diffing (originally Table 6, now Table 1)

2. Ground truth verification for correlations (originally Figure 12 & Table 10, now Figure 3)

3. Hypotheses for correlations (original Table 11 & 12, now Figure 4)

We have also consolidated all references to the Appendix to the end of sections, so that the main text is self-contained. We use the Appendix for additional supporting evidence, prompts, and hyperparameter details. Some reviewers also asked for clarification on the latent labelling procedure, which we now describe in more detail in Section 3. We have rephrased Section 4.3 (clustering) to emphasize the controllability of SAE embeddings.

**False positive rates** (v8eo, N1em)

Some reviewers were concerned about the false positive rate of the SAE method. This is a great point, and we have since added experiments to quantify this for tasks that involve a hypothesis generation step:

1. For dataset diffing (Section 4.1): in our model comparison experiment, we measure the percentage of generated hypotheses that were successfully verified by our LLM judge across all methods (Figure 12). When comparing one model with other models, we find that SAEs are more successful in generating valid hypotheses than LLM baselines. This suggests that they are more robust to noise during the hypothesis generation process, particularly in more complex comparative settings (such as one model vs. all), since these settings require greater specificity and are more sensitive to noisy hypotheses. We include a more detailed analysis in Appendix F.4.

2. For correlations (Section 4.2): we quantify the correctness of SAE-discovered correlations by computing the “true”, judge-verified NPMI between their concepts (Figure 4). We find that SAE-discovered correlations indeed have generally high “true” NPMI, outperforming the LLM baseline.

**Exploring different SAEs** (v8eo, N1em, bVzV)

Our paper currently uses an SAE trained on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. In Figure 6, we have added retrieval results using Goodfire’s Llama 8B SAE, which was trained on LLama-3.1-8B-Instruct. We find that it performs similarly but slightly worse than the 70B SAE on MAP and MAP@50 scores. 

Additionally, given that our work primarily uses SAE latents as text classifiers of properties, we compare the classification performance of SAE latents from 8B and 70B SAEs. We use latent activations to classify dataset documents based on their labels (e.g. “mentions a dog”) and measure “prediction” performance using the “ground-truth” classifications made from a LLM judge. Our preliminary findings suggest that F1 scores improve for the 70B over 8B SAE on datasets similar to the SAE’s training distribution (ie. chat-related data) but remain similar otherwise (Figure 29). This would suggest that a smaller SAE could effectively perform non-chat analyses, which aligns with the new evidence from Figure 6. We provide details for these preliminary findings in Appendix J. 

**Added baselines** (N1em)

We have also added additional baselines for the dataset diffing (Section 4.1) and correlations tasks (Section 4.2).

1. For dataset diffing (Section 4.1), we consider another LLM baseline that generates differences between model responses and uses clustering to form hypotheses (denoted as LLM-C). This differs from our prior baseline (denoted LLM-S), where we generate differences between model responses but use summarization to form hypotheses. While LLM-C generally finds bigger differences than LLM-S, the SAE continues to outperform both baselines (Figure 2).

2. For correlations (Section 4.2), we added a correlated topic model (CTM) baseline to discover topics from word co-occurrences, and we have also streamlined the LLM baseline (standardized the number of texts per batch). The SAE outperforms both baselines.

We believe that our edits have substantially strengthened the paper in both its rigor and clarity. We welcome further comments on the readability of the new manuscript, as well as any more pressing gaps in our experiments.

**The author's use a LLM judge to verify many of the hypothesis generated by the diffing and correlations based methods - although implementation details are unclear**

Thank you for point out this gap in clarity. We have organized the details for verifying hypotheses generated by diffing and correlations-based methods in Section K, and we reference this now at the beginning of Section 4.

**The main text requires constant cross-referencing with the appendix, and key details are often unclear...for example, the latent relabeling procedure, synthetic dataset construction in Section 4.2, what constitutes a "hypothesis," and how hypotheses are verified.**

Thank you for pointing this out. Please see the "Clarity" section of the meta-commentary. In line with your recommendations, we have:

- Consolidated references to the Appendix so the main text is more self-contained

- Added elaboration on the latent labeling procedure in Section 3

- Explained synthetic dataset construction in the main text in Section 4.2
 
- Rephrased Section 4.3 (clustering) to emphasize the controllability of SAE embeddings

Please let us know if there are any parts of the updated manuscript that remain confusing, and we will try our best to correct them for the remainder of the rebuttal period!

**Many results follow a pattern of generating hypotheses, verifying some subset, and presenting the verified ones. It would be helpful to understand the selection process better: what is the false positive rate? How many proposed hypotheses were actually verified?**

Please see the "False positives" section under the meta-commentary.

**For the OpenAI behavior analysis and Tulu-3 data analysis, were the presented results selected from a larger set of hypotheses that were first verified?**

For the OpenAI case study, we first filtered our latents down to those that increase in frequency over model releases. In this case, we mostly looked manually at the latent descriptions and the data itself, finding that we were able to extract a diverse range of patterns relatively easily. We expand on methodological details in Appendix C.1. 

For the Tulu case study, we only presented the “math and hope” correlation as it was one of the most highly correlated (and was among the first ones we found). We focused on this one example to illustrate what an exploratory investigation using SAE embeddings would look like. It is likely that there are more we missed that we leave for future work.

**Was the choice to present only Grok4 behavior diffing results because it had the most differences, or because the other diffed models lacked different behaviors?**

A prior version of the manuscript didn’t include the valid hypotheses generated for all settings (an oversight on our end); we have since updated Appendix F.4 with all valid hypotheses generated from SAEs and our two baselines (see Table 7-9). If you are clarifying why we selected Grok-4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and GPT-OSS-120B in our multi-model settings, we chose to feature these models because they were (at the time of testing) newly released models that had notable differences with other models.

**Some applications feel less compelling and distract from the stronger results...the correlation findings reflect obvious dataset structure...the clustering results aren't falsified or verified, and they don't demonstrate the key advantage of SAE embeddings—the ability to cluster on specific interpretable concepts**

We agree that the correlation findings reflect obvious dataset structure if we know a priori that the Pile contains these types of documents. However, the strength of the method is that we are able to discover these correlations between arbitrary features with no priors, and this example shows that it is possible (for a case where we know the ground truth of why these correlations exist). Furthermore, we included this example to highlight the diversity of SAE features and, thus, possible hypotheses e.g. the StackExchange correlation is between a formatting feature (Q&A) and conceptual features (code, previous attempts). 

For clustering, we clarify that we did evaluate our clustering using the per-cluster accuracy: given a clustering and its cluster descriptions, we asked an LLM to assign each text to one cluster using only these descriptions, then compute the fraction of texts from the original cluster that remain. This quantifies “how coherent is this cluster to its supposed meaning”, and we did quantify this for various datasets. However, we have since taken your feedback into consideration and reorganized the clustering section to focus more on controllability, as we agree that it is one of the key advantages of SAEs.

**Many of the key results...are placed in the appendix rather than integrated into the main text...the figure that explains the flow for each of the analysis tasks (Figure 8) is also in the appendix**

Please see the "Clarity" section in the meta-commentary. We did not include the methods figure (originally Figure 8, currently figure 10) due to space constraints and instead explain the methodology in the experiment setup of each section. We hope that the current version’s description of the methods in the main text is sufficient to understand the flow, and we’d be happy to clarify things further if needed.

**In section 3, the paper does not describe how “activating examples” for a latent are selected**

Thank you for bringing this up. We have added more detail on the SAE labelling pipeline in Section 3: the activating examples for a latent are randomly sampled, then given to an LLM to infer the common feature that the latent represents. 

**The claimed 2-8x cost improvements appear less compelling since it is demonstrated only for the dataset diffing...it feels somewhat misleading...clustering...actually shows an increase in computational cost.**

Our 2-8x claim applies to data diffing in this work and is intended to show that SAE embeddings are cheaper than LLM-based analysis methods, not dense embeddings. While we do not show this cost analysis for the correlations task (since the LLM methods here are less well-established), our cost advantage is more closely tied to the reusable nature of embeddings themselves, rather than with a SAE. For instance, in Section 5.1’s OpenAI case study, we find latent pairs that are increasingly correlated over time to discover more frequent qualities under specific prompt categories. If we were to apply a small variation to our question (e.g. which qualities are $\textit{decreasing}$ over time?), we could reuse our SAE embeddings. Theoretically, it is possible to apply a similar LLM baseline shown in Section 4.2—directly prompting the dataset for interesting correlations—but we’d need to repeat this step for each new question, which becomes problematic for very large datasets. 

However, we acknowledge the confusion and have more explicitly clarified in the limitations that for clustering and retrieval tasks, the SAE embedding is more computationally expensive than traditional dense embeddings due to the larger model and added step of dense embeddings of the labels. 

**Further, each task involves a fairly complex workflow and consequently could introduce compounding errors at multiple stages**

We acknowledge this concern. For each task, we first verify that SAEs can recover ground-truth labels. We tried to simplify the methods as much as possible for the ground-truth evaluations to test the fundamental capabilities of SAEs (ex. for diffing, we exclude any latent relabeling), before moving on to complex, real-world settings where debugging is more difficult

**Are the relabelling costs included in the SAE method in Table 2?**

Yes. Table 2 combines the token counts for all stages of the pipeline, including creating the SAE embedding (w/ LLama-70B) and relabeling the latents (w/ Gemini 2.5 Flash). For clarity, we provide a breakdown of the token counts by model in Table 6, and we would be happy to hear any suggestions on clearer ways to present the total token cost.

**Is the precision for all tasks affected when the SAE training distribution differs..from the distribution of the target datasets?**

For each task, we include analysis examples beyond just model data. To name a few:

- In Section 4.1, we apply dataset diffing on a movie genre dataset and show how it can recover the genre labels.

- In Section 4.2, we find correlated latent pairs in CivilComments, surfacing instances of toxicity and bias.

- In Appendix H.3, we cluster IMDb movie descriptions, showing how SAEs naturally cluster by language style and can also be controlled to cluster by character descriptions instead

- In Section 4.4, we include non-model data in our benchmarks, such as arXiv q-bio abstracts, and show that SAE embeddings are still on par with or outperform dense embedding baselines.

These examples show that SAE embeddings are still performant for their tasks even when the target datasets do not align with the SAE’s training distribution. They also align with our preliminary findings in Appendix J, where we use latent activations to classify documents from various datasets—chat and non-chat—and get a similar F1 score using LLM judge classifications as the ground truth (Figure 30). We would be excited to see more work done on how SAE embeddings perform under OOD distributions. 

In conclusion, we thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback. Their suggestions have prompted numerous experiments that we have added to the paper. We have also moved key figures from the appendix to the main text to improve readability. We hope these improvements are clear and satisfactory for the reviewer.

summary.value:
- The authors propose using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to generate interpretable text embeddings. Each SAE feature corresponds to an embedding dimension created by max pooling that feature's activations over a document, yielding embeddings where each dimension has a natural semantic interpretation.
- The authors demonstrate four applications of SAE embeddings: (1) data diffing to identify differences between text corpora, (2) discovering unexpected correlations between features, (3) clustering, and (4) retrieval.
- For each application, the authors provide both toy setting with known ground truth and open-ended exploratory analyses. In toy settings, they compare SAE embedding performance to corresponding dense embedding or LLM-based baselines.
- The authors lastly present two case studies: analyzing changes in OpenAI model behavior over time using data diffing, and discovering unexpected feature correlations in Tulu-3's post-training dataset.

strengths.value:
- The idea of using SAEs to generate interpretable text embeddings feels novel and well-motivated.
- The authors cover an wide breadth of applications - data diffing, correlation discovery, clustering, and retrieval.
- The experiments have great coverage, including both toy settings with ground truth targets and real-world exploratory analyses. The authors make a solid effort to incorporate baselines (dense embeddings and LLM-based methods) for comparison.
- The real-world case studies find some interesting behaviors in deployed models (Grok, OpenAI models over time, Tulu-3)
- The author's use a LLM judge to verify many of the hypothesis generated by the diffing and correlations based methods - although implementation details are unclear

weaknesses.value:
- The paper's breadth makes it challenging to communicate each experiment with sufficient depth. The main text requires constant cross-referencing with the appendix, and key details are often unclear or left for the reader to infer—for example, the latent relabeling procedure, synthetic dataset construction in Section 4.2, what constitutes a "hypothesis," and how hypotheses are verified.
- Many results follow a pattern of generating hypotheses, verifying some subset, and presenting the verified ones. It would be helpful to understand the selection process better: what is the false positive rate? How many proposed hypotheses were actually verified? Providing this context would help assess whether the positive results shown are representative or cherry-picked.
- Some applications feel less compelling and distract from the stronger results. For instance, the correlation findings reflect obvious dataset structure (e.g., Stack Exchange containing both QA and code). Similarly, the clustering results aren't falsified or verified, and they don't demonstrate the key advantage of SAE embeddings—the ability to cluster on specific interpretable concepts—instead just showing that SAE and dense embeddings produce different clusters.

Overall: my main concerns are about presentation and prioritization rather than the method or experiments themselves. Substantial revision for clarity would improve my assessment of the paper.

questions.value:
- Can you provide more detail about the false-positive rate of hypotheses generated by your method? For the OpenAI behavior analysis and Tulu-3 data analysis, were the presented results selected from a larger set of hypotheses that were first verified? Understanding the selection process would help assess how representative these findings are. Similarly, was the choice to present only Grok4 behavior diffing results because it had the most differences, or because the other diffed models lacked different behaviors?
- You currently use one SAE configuration on one model, which is reasonable for a proof of concept. Do you have any preliminary experiments or intuitions about how method performance might change with different SAE configurations—both in terms of dictionary size and the size/complexity of the underlying model?
- Regarding the token usage comparisons in Table 2, as I understand it, the SAE tokens appear to be from Llama-70B, while the LLM baseline tokens are from whatever frontier model is used to review/process the data (Gemini 2 Flash). This does not seem to be a fair comparison unless I am missing something.

Thank you for your detailed feedback. We address each of your points below:

**Diffing: Table 6 provides a qualitative sanity check but lacks a quantitative...evaluation. Adding [it]..along with a comparison to the LLM baseline would increase the reliability of the claim.**

Thank you for the suggestion! To quantitatively evaluate SAEs on their ability to recover the ground truth (either the “tone” or the “genre” in our two datasets), we measure the surface similarity between the top five SAE latent differences and the ground truth label (e.g. “friendly-and-personable”). We pass in the descriptions and ground truth and prompt GPT-5 to compare them (1 = same, 0.5 = related, 0 = unrelated), following Movva et. al. [1]. 

We compute the surface similarity for thirteen tones and nineteen genres. Using SAEs, we get an average score of 0.75 for the movies dataset and 0.8 for the tones dataset, indicating that SAEs can recover the ground truth as our qualitative sanity check showed. We brought what was previously Table 6 (which shows the top latent differences) from the appendix, so note that it is now Table 1.

We also consider a simple LLM baseline, where we pass in two datasets (e.g. the “action” movie descriptions and 500 random other descriptions) into a LLM and prompt it for the main difference. As the tone and movies dataset are fairly small, they fit into the context window without batching. This baseline achieves an average score of 0.90 for the movies dataset and 0.78 for the tones dataset, showing that LLMs can also recover the ground truth. However, we note that this was a simpler problem to analyze, given the small dataset sizes, and we more rigorously compare SAEs and LLM methods in noisy real-world settings like model diffing. We have added the SAE result in Section 4.1 and LLM baseline results in Appendix F.3.

**Diffing: In Figure 2, the effect of correlated or redundant latents on difference detection is not analyzed. SAEs tend to produce correlated latents, and one should account for their impact on frequency differences.**

Thank you for bringing up this point. Our pipeline involves a summarization step for the top latent differences, where we include an instruction to produce distinct hypotheses (prompt in Appendix F.2). For reference, Table 7 shows all generated hypotheses from the SAE. In Figure 13, we additionally measure how well the overall set of hypotheses distinguishes the unique qualities of our target dataset by computing the percentage of responses where at least one hypothesis uniquely applies to the target model's response. 

We find that SAE hypotheses have greater coverage than baseline hypotheses on multi-model settings and similar or slightly worse coverage on two-model settings. We also observe that SAEs have better success generating valid hypotheses on multi-model settings than two-model settings when compared with LLMs (Figure 12). We suspect this is because the differences in the multi-model settings are more granular and harder to spot (e.g. Gemini 2.5 Pro has certain catchphrases like “Of course!”). Since SAE latents naturally group documents by a property like “introductory remarks”, it is easier to identify dataset trends. In contrast, these patterns may be scattered for LLMs when they summarize observed differences, leading to broad or vague hypotheses that don’t uniquely apply to the target model. Together, these results suggest that SAEs are particularly effective at finding valid hypotheses in more complicated comparisons like the multi-model setting. In simpler two-dataset comparisons, SAEs are on par with LLM baselines at a significantly lower cost. 

**Correlations...lacks a quantitative evaluation of its signal-to-noise ratio. Quantifying the proportion of trivial or false-positive correlations would help in assessing the method’s practical utility and how much manual checking is required**

Please see the "false positive rates" section in the meta-commentary.

In terms of the method's practical utility, it is harder to quantify how often we find "interesting" or surprising correlations as a dataset may not have “interesting correlations” (it could, in truth, have only very few). Given our hyperparameter setup, we got 759 latent pairs for CivilComments and 1283 pairs for the Pile, which is indeed a large number of pairs due to how fine-grained the SAE latents are. The hypotheses we presented for CivilComments and the Pile were generated from manual scanning of these latent pairs and are not exhaustive, but they serve as examples of “interesting”, verified real-world correlations.

Thank you for acknowledging the interesting nature of our analysis! We have addressed each of your points below:

**Organization and readability can be improved; heavy cross-referencing to tables/figures disrupts flow. A streamlined structure would significantly help comprehension.**

Thank you for raising this. Please see the "Clarity" section in the meta-commentary.

**The procedure for producing interpretable activation vectors is not very clear. I am confused about how to define the meanings for each feature. For example, in Fig. 1, why does “feature 1” correspond to nouns and “feature 2” to animals?**

We have expanded on the SAE labelling pipeline in section 3. The SAE sparsity penalty results in latents that tend to correspond to human-interpretable concepts: in other words, if you collect all the tokens a specific latent activates on, they (and their prior context) tend to be related.

A latent is labelled as follows:

- Sample 10 activating phrases and 10 non-activating phrases for that latent. The activating phrases are likely to share some common feature, which is what the latent represents. 

- Give an LLM these phrases, and ask it to generate a label that captures the feature present in the activating phrases. 

One can do this for every latent in an SAE, obtaining a fixed set of labels that create a mapping between a dimension in the SAE embedding and a semantic property like “mentions of dogs”. Any document’s SAE embedding can thus be understood using these labels.

We also clarify that Figure 1 does not depict real SAE latents, but just some toy examples (e.g. “animals” as a placeholder for a non-activating latent for the text “SAEs are useful”). We chose those toy examples to demonstrate how empirically, there are many different types of SAE latents (e.g. “nouns”/”verbs” for part of speech, “animals/technical terms” for specific token-level concepts, “making a claim” for broader concepts), which activate when their associated concept is present. We’ve now explicitly stated in the caption that it is a toy example.

**How are 61,521 latent descriptions obtained from a dictionary of size 65,536? What is the exact pipeline for deriving concrete descriptions per feature?**

The Goodfire SAEs come with 61,521 labels that the Goodfire team created, likely using auto-interpretability techniques on the LMSYS-1M dataset. It is not fully clear why some labels were not provided, but we point to their public statement explaining that “a significant portion of harmful features” were removed prior to release [1]. We have more explicitly stated this as a footnote on page 3.

We use these existing labels for many of our analyses (e.g. correlations, clustering, retrieval), but we can also create more precise labels using the pipeline described above.

Thank you for your helpful clarifications! We hope that the methodology is a lot clearer now, and we hope the reviewer will reconsider their evaluation.

[1] McGrath et. al. https://www.goodfire.ai/research/understanding-and-steering-llama-3

summary.value: This paper utilizes pretrained SAEs' latens to build an embedding model that is able to capture property of interest and also allows interpretability whereas dense embedding models lack both, and are trained to capture semantics which does not allow full controllabilitiy. With their methodology, they are capable of doing dataset diffing more efficiently and accurately and it enables exploration of unknown correlation between different concepts that are often missed by LLMs. Moreover they adapt these embeddings to other downstream tasks such as clustering and retrieval. Lastly, they analyze two case studies which are the behavior change of openai models illustrated by their personification ability, and analysis of tulu3 sft data in which they find that math/latex like concepts correlate with the hoping and they are able to trigger this behaviour by using the correlated concepts. Overall, they modify the popular SAE framework-which is primarily used to investigate model behaviour- to generate embeddings that could be used in various NLP tasks while often outperforming or being on par with LLMs or dense embedding models.

summary.value: This paper explores the use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) trained on LLM hidden states to create interpretable embeddings for text data. Each dimension in the SAE embedding is supposed to represent a human-interpretable feature, which the authors use for four text analysis tasks: comparing datasets, finding correlations, clustering, and property-based retrieval. The paper presents two important case studies: The first tracks behavioral changes across ChatGPT versions, showing increasing nuance and self-critique in responses, more personalized follow-ups, and descriptions that personify objects more frequently. The second analyzes Tulu-3’s fine-tuning data and finds that certain prompt formats, such as numbered lists, LaTeX math, and role-playing instructions, consistently cause it to end with the phrase “I hope it is correct.” The paper traces this to a specific training subset and confirm that these prompt patterns directly trigger the behavior in the Tulu-3 model.

strengths.value:
The paper introduces a novel and creative application of SAEs beyond their typical role in LLM interpretability to the domain of textual data analysis. I think SAEs are a great choice as a data analysis toolkit for the following reasons:  the interpretable and sparse embeddings offer greater controllability compared to dense embeddings, like enabling pre-filtering of features for targeted analysis of specific properties. Further, SAEs can capture implicit features of chat dialogues beyond coarse semantic content, e.g., sycophancy, anthropomorphism, or the presence of reasoning chains, which dense embedding models typically miss. This makes them a better candidate for analysing model training data/responses

The real-world use cases presented in the paper are great illustrations of the method’s practicality. Additionally, this paper presents a promising direction for unstructured data analysis of model-related data and might encourage interesting future research.

weaknesses.value:
Overall, the experiments lack rigor, and the work feels preliminary (details below). I see this paper as a good proof-of-concept, and in its current state, it is more suitable for a workshop or a blog post.

I have listed some weaknesses along with some suggestions below (loosely in order of priority). Many of them are related to the four data analysis tasks. Personally, I think these tasks could be removed altogether. The paper would be stronger if it focused more on the case studies instead. You could then consider organizing the findings into clearer categories, such as debugging fine-tuning data or understanding model behavior both within and across model families.

* Table 6 provides a qualitative sanity check but lacks a quantitative or statistically grounded evaluation. Adding a measurable metric along with a comparison to the LLM baseline would increase the reliability of the claim.
* The correlation discovery method in Section 4.2 lacks a quantitative evaluation of its signal-to-noise ratio. Quantifying the proportion of trivial or false-positive correlations would help in assessing the method’s practical utility and how much manual checking is required
* In Section 4.4, the SAE retrieval setup introduces higher computational overhead due to latent-query dense similarity matching. Exploring alternative strategies that are more efficient would make the method more practical for real-world deployment.
* In Figure 2, the effect of correlated or redundant latents on difference detection is not analyzed. SAEs tend to produce correlated latents, and one should account for their impact on frequency differences.
* In Section 4.3, clustering results are only reported for one algorithm. Demonstrating consistent results across multiple algorithms would increase the reliability of the claim.
* Results are reported for only one SAE model. Testing multiple SAE models would make the findings more reliable and better support the claim that SAEs are a good choice.
* Prompt variation effects across all experiments are not studied. Testing different prompt formulations for the LLM stages and baselines would clarify how sensitive the results are to prompt design.
* The analysis workflows depend heavily on another LLM to summarize or relabel latent features, suggesting that SAEs alone are not sufficient for the intended tasks. Designing experiments that evaluate the effectiveness of SAEs in isolation would provide a clearer understanding of their independent capabilities and limitations.
* Many of the key results (Table 6, Figure 12, Table 10, Table 11, Table 12, Figure 13) are placed in the appendix rather than integrated into the main text. Bringing these results forward would make the paper’s main findings more accessible. For instance, while reading the paper, I had to move back and forth multiple times just to understand the results of each experiment. In similar vein, the figure that explains the flow for each of the analysis tasks (Figure 8) is also in the appendix. Including this figure in the main text would improve readability.
* In section 3, the paper does not describe how “activating examples” for a latent are selected. Describing the process would help better understand the SAE pipeline.
* The claimed 2-8x cost improvements appear less compelling since it is demonstrated only for the dataset diffing experiment. In fact, it feels somewhat misleading, as the clustering experiment actually shows an increase in computational cost.

Further, each task involves a fairly complex workflow and consequently could introduce compounding errors at multiple stages.

summary.value:
Large-scale text corpora analysis is challenging. This paper proposes using Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) to create interpretable embeddings for analyzing large corpora. 
Extensive quantitative experiments suggest that SAE embeddings are useful and versatile tools for data analysis, benefiting multiple applications, including dataset diffing, correlation, clustering, and retrieval.

strengths.value:

- Compared to LLM-based inspection, SAEs are more economical, particularly for data diffing tasks.
- Experiments are detailed and (apparently) easy to reproduce, improving credibility and reusability.

summary.value: The reviewers broadly agree that the paper is a novel, creative application of SAEs, with interesting real-world case studies. Several reviewers view the approach as promising and practically useful for analyzing large, unstructured corpora. However, there is substantial disagreement about experimental rigor and maturity: the key disagreement is about whether the SAEs, rather than the surrounding LLM framework, are responsible for the paper’s claimed analytical capabilities.

reviewer_concerns.value:
A common concern raised by all reviewers was clarity and organization. Issues include heavy reliance on the appendix as well as vague descriptions of the SAE labeling and hypothesis-verification pipelines. These concerns have largely been addressed.

The remaining substantive concerns are questions of rigor and validation. Reviewers raised concerns about false positives and selection bias in hypothesis-generation tasks, dependence on LLM judges for labeling and verification, limited ablations, and computational practicality. The rebuttal adds quantitative evaluations of false-positive rates, new baselines, and limited experiments with additional SAEs, which address some but not all of these issues; concerns about prompt sensitivity, correlated latents, clustering robustness, and the extent to which SAEs can be evaluated independently of LLM components are only partially resolved.

comment.value:
**You currently use one SAE configuration on one model, which is reasonable for a proof of concept. Do you have any preliminary experiments or intuitions about how method performance might change with different SAE configurations—both in terms of dictionary size and the size/complexity of the underlying model?**

Please see the "Exploring different SAEs" section in the meta-commentary.

As for dictionary sizes, our intuition is that there is a sweet spot for dictionary size—too small and the latents are too broad, leading to vague hypotheses, but too large and the latents are too fine-grained, leading to noise.

**Regarding the token usage comparisons in Table 2...the SAE tokens appear to be from Llama-70B, while the LLM baseline tokens are from whatever frontier model is used to review/process the data (Gemini 2 Flash). This does not seem to be a fair comparison unless I am missing something.**

Table 2 combines the token counts for all stages of the pipeline, including creating the SAE embedding (w/ LLama-70B) and relabeling the latents (w/ Gemini 2.5 Flash). While Table 2 thus mixes different models together, it aims to show that SAEs require far fewer tokens to run than our LLM baselines, which leads to cost and latency benefits. For clarity, we provide a breakdown of the token counts by model in Table 6, and we would be happy to hear any suggestions on clearer ways to present the token cost.

In all, we thank the reviewer for your constructive feedback. We hope that the revised manuscript is clearer and our experiments on false positive rates are satisfactory.
